newsitem.title: USA: Storm pounds New England for third day.
newsitem.headline: Storm pounds New England for third day.

text.p: Record rains and high winds pounded New England for a third day on Monday and a state of emergency was called for flood-ravaged communities in eastern Massachusetts, giving thousands of schoolchildren a day off.

The storm, which lashed New York and New Jersey on Saturday and which authorities there said claimed four lives, has dumped up to 11 inches (27.5 cm) in parts of Massachusetts and caused several rivers to overflow in that state and southeastern New Hampshire since the start of the weekend.

The Taylor River spilled over its banks and onto Interstate 95 in Hampton Falls, New Hampshire, reducing the important north-south highway to one lane, police said. The Neponsett River south of Boston spilled over and officials said they were expecting it to crest at 11 feet (3.3 metres), two feet (0.7 metres) over flood stage some time on Tuesday.

The National Weather Service said Boston's Logan International Airport had received 6.11 inches (15.27 cm) of rain, shattering a 101-year-old record for rainfall in a 24-hour period in October. The previous record, of 4.92 inches (12.26 cm) was set in October 1895.
"If this had been snow, it easily would have been over 100 inches (250 cm)," National Weather Service meterologist Michael Dion said.

Massachusetts Bay Transportation Authority officials were forced to shut down major sections of Boston's subway system when the station at Kenmore Square, an important junction, was under 20 feet (6 metres) of water, a state Emergency Management Agency spokeswoman said. Transportation officials said they did not expect to have the station pumped out until on Tuesday at the earliest.

Gov. William Weld declared a state of emergency on Monday morning for flood-ravaged communities in eastern Massachusetts. Flash flood warnings have been issued and several dams in New England have seen overspill.
The Red Cross set up seven emergency shelters in eastern Massachusetts as more than half a dozen towns in the area have been partially evacuated, spokeswoman Renita Hosler said.
Freemont, New Hampshire had received eight inches (20.3 cm) and East Derry, New Hampshire 6.84 inches (17.4 cm) by 6:00 a.m. EDT as the rain continued, the National Weather Service said.

Winds gusted to 50 mph (80 km) in Portsmouth, New Hampshire and 43 mph (68.8 km) in Portland, Maine. A gust of 115 mph (184 km) was recorded on Mount Washington, the highest point in New England, weather forecasters said.

Central Maine Power Co., which reported 5,000 people were without electricity on Sunday, said repair crews reduced that to only scattered outages on Monday morning despite the tough working conditions.

Thousands of children in eastern New Hampshire, southern Maine and eastern Massachusetts got the day off from school Monday as street flooding made some roadways impassable and others too dangerous for buses, authorities reported.

In Connecticut, Northeast Utilities reported that some 17,000 customers, mostly in Fairfield County near the New York State border, remained without power. Up to 90,000 Northeast customers were without power at some point since the storm struck late on Saturday, spokesman Bruno Ranniello said.
The weather service is predicting the rain will taper off to showers later Monday with clearing expected Tuesday.

The ferocious storm on Saturday dropped record-for-the-date rains in Central Park and Newark and deluged other parts of New Jersey with up to 8.6 inches (21.8 cm), cut power to 341,000 homes in New York, New Jersey and Connecticut, and flooded coasts, rivers and low-lying homes and highways.
